changes.after: An R function normally waits to work out an input until it actually uses that input.

before: A supplied function argument is usually a promise: its expression and calling environment are retained until the value is needed. An unused argument can therefore contain an expression that would fail if evaluated. stop(message) raises an error and interrupts normal execution.

force(x) evaluates the promise for x now. It is useful before returning a closure that should retain the current argument value. It does not recursively force every promise stored elsewhere.

Here force receives the promised x argument and evaluates it even though use is FALSE. The supplied stop call receives a diagnostic message and raises that error, so no value 7 is returned. This deliberately failing example contrasts with the successful lazy call below.
```r
choose_now <- function(x, use) {
  force(x)
  if (use) x else 7
}
choose_now(stop("evaluated"), FALSE)
```
This stops with evaluated.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
choose <- function(x, use) {
  if (use) x else 7
}
cat(choose(stop("evaluated"), FALSE), "\n")
```
Expected output or behavior: 7. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Replace stop with a visible message and compare the timing with and without force. You may trace it without a R interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: An R function normally waits to work out an input until it actually uses that input.
When use is false, this branch returns seven without evaluating x.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```r
choose <- function(x, use) {
  if (use) x else 7
}
cat(choose(stop("evaluated"), FALSE), "\n")
```
The output is `7`. The stop call was supplied as x, but no one asked for its value.
Put force(x) first to request x immediately.
